title: Salt for a Hangover: Does It Help? Salt Water, Broth and Limits
excerpt: Does salt help a hangover? How sodium helps you rehydrate, why salty broth beats salt water, salt cravings after drinking, salt tablets, and who should skip it.
metaDescription: Does salt help a hangover? How sodium helps you rehydrate, why salty broth beats salt water or salt tablets, and who should go easy on extra salt.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** salt can help a hangover a little, but only as part of rehydrating, and only when you've actually lost fluid. A pinch of salt in water, a salty broth, or a few crackers gives your body sodium, and sodium helps your gut pull water in and helps you hold on to the fluid you drink. That's useful if you were sick, sweated a lot dancing, or woke up genuinely dry. What salt can't do is fix the main drivers of a hangover: poor sleep, inflammation, the by-products of breaking down alcohol, and low blood sugar. And more salt is not better. Straight salt water or a handful of salt tablets can make nausea worse and, in large amounts, can be dangerous.

**The quick rules:** If you want to use salt, take it *with* fluid and food, not on its own. A cup of warm broth, a glass of water with a small pinch of salt and a squeeze of citrus, or a properly mixed oral rehydration drink are all reasonable. Don't drink strong salt water, don't take salt tablets "to be safe," and skip extra salt if you have high blood pressure, heart failure, or kidney disease unless your doctor has said otherwise.

> **When to see a doctor.** Most hangovers fade within a day with fluids, food, and rest. **Get medical help if** you can't keep any fluids down for several hours, you're vomiting repeatedly or see blood in your vomit, you're very dizzy or faint when you stand, you're confused or unusually drowsy, you've barely urinated in many hours, or you have chest pain or a racing, irregular heartbeat. If someone who drank heavily can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has bluish or pale skin, or has a seizure, call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away. That's alcohol poisoning, not a hangover. Separately, if you regularly drink a lot and get shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you stop, tell a doctor. Those can be withdrawal signs and are worth taking seriously.

## Does Salt Help a Hangover? What It Can and Can't Do

Salt is sodium chloride. Sodium is the main electrolyte in the fluid around your cells, and it's the one your body uses most to decide how much water to keep. When people say "electrolytes help a hangover," sodium is doing most of the work.

Here's where salt genuinely earns its place:

- **It helps your gut absorb water.** Your small intestine has transporters that move sodium and glucose into the body together, and water follows them. This is the principle behind oral rehydration solution, which the World Health Organization has used for decades to treat dehydration from diarrhea. A drink with a little salt and a little sugar is absorbed better than plain water when you're actually dehydrated.
- **It helps you hold on to fluid.** Plain water on an empty stomach can pass through you quickly. Some sodium alongside it, especially with food, means more of that water stays in your body instead of heading straight to the bathroom.
- **It replaces what you lost if you were sick or sweaty.** Vomiting, diarrhea, and heavy sweating all remove sodium as well as water. In those cases, replacing both makes sense.

Here's where it falls short:

- **Dehydration is only one part of a hangover.** Researchers who study hangovers have found that how dehydrated people are doesn't line up neatly with how bad they feel. Studies measuring blood electrolytes in hungover people have generally not found large differences from normal. That suggests fluid loss contributes to symptoms like thirst, dry mouth, and dizziness, but isn't the root cause of the headache, fatigue, and general misery.
- **Salt does nothing for the other causes.** Alcohol disrupts sleep, triggers an inflammatory response, and is broken down into acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product. It can also drop blood sugar. Salt doesn't touch any of these.
- **Most people already get plenty of sodium.** The typical Western diet is high in salt. Unless you lost a lot of fluid, you probably aren't short on sodium the morning after. You're more likely short on water, sleep, and food.

So the fair answer to "does salt help a hangover" is: it helps your body rehydrate more efficiently, which can ease the thirsty, lightheaded, dried-out part of a hangover. It isn't a cure, and there's no good evidence that salt on its own shortens or prevents a hangover.

## Why Alcohol Leaves You Dried Out

To understand why salt is sometimes useful, it helps to know what alcohol does to your fluid balance.

Normally your brain releases a hormone called vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone) that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. Alcohol suppresses that hormone while your blood alcohol level is rising. Your kidneys then let more water go than they normally would, which is why you find yourself queuing for the bathroom after a few drinks.

On top of that:

- **You may not drink water alongside alcohol**, so you're losing fluid without replacing it.
- **Vomiting and diarrhea** after a heavy night strip out both water and electrolytes, including sodium and potassium.
- **Sweating** in a hot bar, on a dance floor, or in warm weather adds more losses.
- **Sleeping with your mouth open** (common after drinking) leaves you with that parched feeling on waking.

Most of what you lose through extra urination is water rather than a large amount of salt. That's why water is the main fix and salt is a helper. The exception is when you've been sick or sweating heavily, which is when sodium replacement matters more. For more on this, see our guide on [whether alcohol really dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you).

## Salt Water for a Hangover: Is It a Good Idea?

You'll see "drink salt water" recommended online as a hangover hack. It depends a lot on how much salt you mean.

**A tiny pinch in a big glass of water: reasonable.** A small pinch of salt (a fraction of a teaspoon) in a large glass of water, ideally with a squeeze of lemon or a little juice for sugar and flavor, is a rough home version of a rehydration drink. It shouldn't taste salty. If it tastes like seawater, it's far too strong.

**Strong salt water: a bad idea.** Drinking concentrated salt water can irritate your stomach and make you vomit. Doctors used to use salt water to deliberately make people throw up, and they stopped because it caused dangerously high sodium levels in some patients. When you're already nauseous and low on fluid, that's the opposite of what you want.

**Why too much salt backfires:** a very salty drink is more concentrated than your body fluids. Instead of helping you absorb water, it can draw water *into* your gut, which can cause cramping, diarrhea, and more fluid loss. That's the same reason drinking seawater makes thirst worse.

If you want a measured version, our [homemade electrolyte drink guide](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) covers simple ratios. The key point is that a rehydration drink should be mildly salty at most, with some sugar to help the sodium do its job.

## Salty Broth: The Best Way to Use Salt for a Hangover

If you're going to use salt the morning after, a warm cup of broth is probably the best way to do it. It's the one salt-based remedy that lines up well with what the body actually needs.

Why broth works well:

- **It's sodium and water together.** You get the electrolyte and the fluid in one go, which is exactly the combination that helps absorption.
- **It's gentle on a queasy stomach.** Warm, clear liquids are often easier to keep down than a full meal or a sugary sports drink.
- **It's food.** Broth made with bones, chicken, or vegetables gives you a little protein and some calories, which can help if your blood sugar is low.
- **It's easy to sip slowly.** Small sips over 20 to 30 minutes are easier on your stomach than gulping a big glass of anything.

How salty is a cup of broth? It varies a lot by brand. Regular canned or boxed broths often contain several hundred milligrams of sodium per cup, and some contain much more. Low-sodium versions have far less. Check the nutrition label so you know what you're getting, especially if you're watching your salt intake.

Good options include plain chicken broth, bone broth, miso soup, and vegetable broth. If you feel up to it, chicken noodle soup adds easy carbohydrates. Many cultures have their own salty hangover soups, and our roundup of [the best soups for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-soups-for-hangover) covers the options in more detail.

## Why You Crave Salty Food After Drinking

Craving chips, fries, or a salty breakfast the morning after is extremely common. A few things are likely going on, and none of them are fully settled science:

- **Fluid loss can increase salt appetite.** When the body is short on fluid, it can nudge you toward salty foods to help hold on to water.
- **Alcohol can make you hungrier in general.** Research on alcohol and appetite suggests drinking can increase food intake and make high-calorie foods more tempting, both during the night and the next day.
- **Low blood sugar pushes you toward quick energy.** Salty snacks are often also starchy or fatty, which is part of the appeal.
- **Habit and comfort.** Many people simply associate salty, greasy food with "recovery" from a night out.

Listening to the craving in moderation is fine. A salty breakfast with eggs and toast, or some crackers, gives you sodium, carbohydrates, and calories. Our guide to [the best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover) goes through the most useful choices.

The trap is turning the craving into a huge, very salty, very greasy meal on a sensitive stomach. That can leave you bloated, thirstier, and more nauseous, and won't speed recovery.

## Salty Food and Hangover Bloating

Salt helps you hold on to water. That's useful when you're dehydrated, but it's also why a very salty meal can leave you puffy. Alcohol can already cause facial puffiness and a bloated feeling, partly through fluid shifts and inflammation. Piling a lot of extra salt on top can make that more noticeable.

If you wake up puffy rather than dry:

- Favor water and water-rich foods like fruit over very salty takeout.
- Don't avoid salt completely, but keep portions normal.
- Potassium-rich foods like bananas, potatoes, oranges, and yogurt help balance sodium.
- Gentle movement and time usually resolve it within a day.

We cover the causes and fixes in more detail in our guide to [alcohol face bloating](/never-hungover/alcohol-face-bloating).

## Salt Tablets for a Hangover: Skip Them

Salt tablets are designed for situations where people lose large amounts of sodium through sweat, such as long endurance events or heavy physical work in hot weather. A typical hangover isn't that situation.

The problems with taking salt tablets for a hangover:

- **They deliver a concentrated dose of sodium all at once**, which can upset an already irritated stomach and trigger nausea or vomiting.
- **Without enough fluid, they can make dehydration feel worse**, because you need water to absorb and balance that sodium.
- **They add to an already high daily sodium intake** for most people.
- **They're risky for some people**, including those with high blood pressure, heart failure, or kidney disease.

If you want measured electrolytes, a properly formulated rehydration drink is a better tool. It's designed to be absorbed well, and you can see exactly how much sodium you're getting.

## How Salt Compares to Other Hangover Electrolyte Options

Here's how common salt sources compare. Sodium content varies by brand and recipe, so treat these as general descriptions and check the label.

| Option | What you get | Best for | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pinch of salt in water with citrus | A little sodium, some flavor, almost no sugar unless you add juice | A cheap, quick home option | Too much salt makes it unpleasant and counterproductive |
| Warm broth or miso soup | Sodium, fluid, some protein and calories | Queasy mornings, gentle refueling | Regular versions can be high in sodium |
| Oral rehydration solution (like Pedialyte) | A measured mix of sodium, potassium, and sugar designed for absorption | After vomiting, diarrhea, or heavy sweating | Can taste salty; more than most people need after a mild night |
| Sports drinks (like Gatorade) | Fluid, sugar, and a modest amount of sodium | Mild dehydration, taste preference | More sugar and less sodium than rehydration drinks |
| Electrolyte powders (like Liquid IV or LMNT) | Varies by product; some are high in sodium | Convenient, measured dosing | Check the sodium per serving; some are very high |
| Pickle juice | Sodium in a salty, vinegary brine | People who like it | Strong taste, high sodium, can irritate the stomach |
| Salty snacks (crackers, pretzels) | Sodium plus easy carbohydrates | Light, bland food when nauseous | Easy to overdo; you still need fluid |
| Salt tablets | Concentrated sodium | Endurance athletes, not hangovers | Nausea, too much sodium, not designed for this |

If you're curious about specific options, we've written separate guides on [pickle juice for a hangover](/never-hungover/pickle-juice-for-hangover), [Liquid IV for a hangover](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-for-hangover), and [the best electrolyte drinks compared](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared).

## How Much Salt Is Too Much?

For a healthy adult, the main US guideline is to keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day, which is roughly the amount in one teaspoon of table salt. The American Heart Association suggests an ideal limit closer to 1,500 mg a day for most adults, especially those with high blood pressure. Most people already eat more than these amounts on an ordinary day.

That puts hangover salt in perspective. You don't need to "load up." A few hundred milligrams of sodium from a cup of broth or a rehydration drink, alongside plenty of fluid, is plenty for most mild-to-moderate hangovers. If you were sick several times, a properly mixed oral rehydration solution is a better choice than guessing with the salt shaker.

Signs you've overdone it include feeling more thirsty, bloated, or nauseous after salty food or drinks. In rare cases, very large amounts of salt taken quickly can raise blood sodium to dangerous levels, causing confusion, muscle twitching, or seizures. That kind of overload is unusual from normal food, but it's why salt water and salt tablets aren't good hangover tools.

## Who Should Be Careful With Extra Salt

Talk to your doctor before using salt, salty broth, or high-sodium electrolyte products as a regular hangover remedy if you:

- **Have high blood pressure.** Extra sodium can push blood pressure up, and alcohol can also raise it.
- **Have heart failure.** Sodium causes the body to hold fluid, which can strain the heart.
- **Have kidney disease.** Your kidneys may not clear extra sodium well.
- **Have liver disease**, especially if you've been told to limit salt.
- **Take medicines that affect sodium or fluid balance**, such as diuretics (water pills), some blood pressure medicines, or certain antidepressants.
- **Have been told to follow a low-sodium diet** for any reason.

For these groups, plain water, low-sodium broth, and simple food are usually safer. A pharmacist can tell you whether a specific electrolyte product is a good fit for you.

## A Simple Morning-After Plan Using Salt Sensibly

If you wake up hungover and want to use salt in a helpful way, here's a straightforward approach:

1. **Start with water.** Sip a glass or two slowly rather than gulping, especially if you feel queasy.
2. **Add some sodium with fluid.** A cup of warm broth is the easiest option. Alternatively, have a rehydration drink or a glass of water with a small pinch of salt and some citrus.
3. **Eat something bland and salty-ish.** Crackers, toast, eggs, or a banana with a few pretzels give you carbohydrates and a little sodium.
4. **Keep sipping through the morning.** Pale yellow urine is a reasonable sign you're catching up on fluid.
5. **Rest.** Sleep debt is a big part of how a hangover feels, and nothing you drink or eat fixes that as well as rest.
6. **Use a stronger rehydration drink only if you were sick.** After vomiting or diarrhea, an oral rehydration solution is designed to replace what you lost.

For a full step-by-step guide to fluids, see [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking). If nausea is your main problem, our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers ways to settle your stomach.

## Can Salt Before Drinking Prevent a Hangover?

There's no good evidence that eating salt before drinking prevents a hangover. What does help is eating a proper meal before and while you drink. Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream, which tends to mean a lower peak blood alcohol level.

There's one salt-related trap worth knowing about. Salty snacks make you thirsty, and if the nearest drink is alcohol, you may drink more and faster. Bars serving free salty snacks is not an accident. If you're snacking on salty food while drinking, alternate with water.

And the salt on a tequila shot or a margarita rim doesn't change anything. It's there for taste, not protection.

For the habits with the best evidence, including pacing, eating, and choosing drinks carefully, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Where DHM Fits In

Salt and water help with the dehydrated side of a hangover. They don't affect how your body processes alcohol. That's where some people look at supplements.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers on its own, and it's not a replacement for pacing yourself, eating, and drinking water.

If you want to try it, it fits alongside the basics rather than instead of them. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which also includes electrolytes, and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take medication, check with a pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- Salt can help a hangover modestly by helping your body absorb and keep the water you drink.
- It works best with fluid and food: warm broth, a lightly salted drink with citrus, or bland salty snacks.
- It doesn't address the main causes of a hangover, such as poor sleep, inflammation, and alcohol by-products.
- Don't drink strong salt water or take salt tablets. Too much salt can worsen nausea and dehydration.
- If you were sick or sweated heavily, a proper oral rehydration solution is a better tool than the salt shaker.
- If you have high blood pressure, heart, kidney, or liver disease, check with your doctor before adding salt.
- If you can't keep fluids down, are confused, or have warning signs of alcohol poisoning, get medical help.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does salt help a hangover?**

Salt can help a little, mainly by helping your body absorb and retain water. Sodium and glucose are absorbed together in the gut, and water follows them, which is why a lightly salted drink or broth can rehydrate you more efficiently than plain water when you're dehydrated. But dehydration is only one part of a hangover, and salt doesn't affect poor sleep, inflammation, or alcohol by-products. Think of it as a rehydration helper, not a cure.

**Is drinking salt water good for a hangover?**

Only if it's very weak. A small pinch of salt in a large glass of water, ideally with a squeeze of citrus or a little juice, can work as a rough rehydration drink. Strong salt water is a bad idea. It can irritate your stomach, cause vomiting or diarrhea, and in large amounts raise blood sodium to dangerous levels. If it tastes noticeably salty, it's too strong.

**Is salty broth good for a hangover?**

Yes, warm broth is one of the better ways to use salt the morning after. It gives you sodium and fluid together, it's gentle on a queasy stomach, and it provides a little protein and calories. Sip it slowly. Check the label if you're watching your sodium intake, because regular broths can be high in salt, and low-sodium versions are available.

**Why do I crave salty food after drinking?**

Several things probably contribute: fluid loss can increase salt appetite, alcohol tends to make you hungrier in general, low blood sugar pushes you toward quick energy, and many people simply associate salty food with recovery. A moderately salty breakfast is fine. A huge greasy, salty meal on a sensitive stomach can leave you bloated and more nauseous.

**Should I take salt tablets for a hangover?**

No. Salt tablets are designed for people who lose a lot of sodium through heavy sweating, such as endurance athletes. For a hangover they deliver too much sodium at once, can upset your stomach, and can make you feel worse if you don't drink enough water with them. A properly mixed rehydration drink is a better choice if you need electrolytes.

**Does eating salt before drinking prevent a hangover?**

There's no good evidence that it does. Eating a full meal before and while drinking helps by slowing alcohol absorption, but salt itself doesn't prevent a hangover. Salty snacks can actually make you thirstier and lead you to drink more alcohol, so alternate with water if you're snacking.

**Is salt or Pedialyte better for a hangover?**

If you were sick or sweated heavily, an oral rehydration solution like Pedialyte is the better option because it combines sodium, potassium, and sugar in amounts designed for absorption. After a milder night, water plus a cup of broth or some salty crackers is usually enough. Neither one cures a hangover.

**Who should avoid extra salt when hungover?**

People with high blood pressure, heart failure, kidney disease, or liver disease, and anyone on a doctor-recommended low-sodium diet or taking medicines that affect sodium or fluid balance, such as diuretics. For these groups, plain water, low-sodium broth, and simple foods are usually safer. Ask a doctor or pharmacist before using high-sodium electrolyte products.
